headline: The Ledge Went Cold and Green Again — Bass Deep, Bonito Scouts Showing South
subhead: Full moon current is stacking bait on the Southwest Ledge and North Rip while the season's first bonito nose into the corridors south of the island.
body_markdown:
You feel the change before you see it out here. I was running out past the breakwater before first light Wednesday and the air over the water had that clean, mineral cold to it — the kind that tells you the upwelling is working before you ever drop a temp gauge. That's the Southwest Ledge doing what it does every August when the moon gets big and the current starts hauling. Cold, oxygen-rich water gets pulled up out of the depths and it stacks bait right on the edge of the structure. When that happens here, the striped bass don't wander far from it.

This week's full moon has put some real muscle into the tide, and that's exactly the kind of current that sharpens up the bite around the Ledge and the North Rip. Daytime action anywhere else on the East Coast right now is mostly dead — the peak-summer heat has bass everywhere from Jersey to the Cape pinned into a strict low-light pattern, holding tight in cooler water and only really feeding at dawn, dusk, and after dark. Block Island is a little different because we've got that natural refrigeration system built into the bottom. The Ledge and the Rip stay charged with cold, moving water around the clock, so we're getting bites through the day that boats working warmer inshore water simply aren't seeing.

Best fish this week came off the Southwest Ledge in 25 to 40 feet, working the last two hours of the ebb into the start of the flood — that current reversal is when the bass really come up off the bottom and start working the edge. Guys jigging 2- to 3-ounce diamond jigs tipped with a squid strip have been connecting, and a few boats trolling umbrella rigs and big parachutes through the deeper water off the Ledge have put 30-plus-pound fish in the box. I had a 40-pounder come off the North Rip Tuesday morning on a chunk of fresh bunker, fished on a fish-finder rig right on bottom in that fast water where the rip stands up — that fish never left the structure, just sat there waiting for the current to bring dinner to him. That's the whole story of this place. You're not searching for bass around Block Island in summer, you're finding the cold water and the bait, and the fish are already there.

Squid have been thick around the island this month, and that's been carrying a lot of this bite. Where you find squid concentrations on the sounder, especially around the Ledge and out toward the East Grounds, you'll usually find bass and blackfish working underneath them. Sea bass have stayed dependable on the reef structure off the south side — jigging bucktails tipped with squid strips in 40 to 60 feet has been steady, nothing spectacular, but a reliable box-filler if the bass bite is slow.

Bluefish have been mixed into the same water, chopping up the bunker schools that push through the rips on the tide changes. Nothing like the giant blitzes you get up at Montauk or Sandy Hook, but enough cocktail blues around to keep rods bent if you're throwing poppers or small metal off the back of the boat while you wait for the tide to turn. Fluke fishing has been the honest, dependable piece of the week — drifting the drop-offs and current-swept edges around the harbor and the south side with Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails has produced a decent number of keepers, though you need to work the tide changes hard. The doormats are holding tight to the cooler water on the edges, same story as everywhere else this time of year.

Now here's the one I've been waiting to write. We flagged it last week — said the water on the south side was closing in on that bonito threshold and the first scouts wouldn't be far behind — and sure enough, there's early bonito showing at the classic corridors: the Race, Fishers Island Sound, and pushing into the Vineyard's south side. Nothing consistent yet around the island itself, but Montauk's holding water in the mid-70s and that warmth is working its way up the coast. If the pattern holds the way it usually does, we should start seeing real bonito and the first false albacore push into Block Island waters within the next couple weeks, especially once that warm water settles into the south-side rips.

Looking ahead, the moon will start easing off full over the next few days, which usually calms the exaggerated current we've had and settles the bite back into a more standard rhythm — still good, just less dramatic swings at the tide changes. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd fish the Southwest Ledge on the last of the ebb into the flood turn, right at first light, with a bucktail or a live eel worked slow along the bottom edge. That's where the cold water, the bait, and the big fish all come together right now. Keep an eye on the south side corridors too — once that bonito shows up in real numbers around the island, it's going to happen fast, and you don't want to be the last boat to hear about it.
